sections.title: The matchup — Cincinnati’s front versus Pittsburgh’s protection
sections.text: Cincinnati has eight sacks through two games and has allowed 74.5 rushing yards per game. Pittsburgh has surrendered six sacks. Cincinnati’s ability to stop early-down runs and create passing situations is a reason to question a large Pittsburgh scoring rebound. These are only two games, so they do not establish a settled team strength.

sections.title: What supports Pittsburgh — and what challenges it
sections.text: Pittsburgh lost 20–3 last week, but seven New England points came from a fumble-return touchdown. Pittsburgh’s defense produced three sacks and two takeaways; that supports a close-game path. Its offense converted just 2 of 12 third downs and allowed four sacks. The defense keeping Cincinnati close is more defensible than assuming the offense immediately recovers.

sections.title: Receivers, protection and special teams
sections.text: Chase and Higgins have productive histories against Pittsburgh. Watt is the pressure threat, while Cincinnati’s Mims has allowed no pressures in 72 pass-blocking snaps this season. McPherson has made all six field-goal attempts. Those matchups and kicking execution matter beyond a quarterback-only comparison.

sections.title: Availability — Friday report, not game-day confirmation
sections.text: Pittsburgh listed Warren, Pittman, Porter and Dean questionable; Dowdle and Dunker were out. Cincinnati listed Iosivas out and B.J. Hill doubtful. Check confirmed game-day availability before relying on those matchups. An injury is a context change, not an automatic instruction to pass.
